::: {.notes}
Jessica Marie Johnson is an Associate Professor of History and the Director of the Program in Africana Studies at Johns Hopkins University. She is the author of *Wicked Flesh: Black Women, Intimacy, and Freedom in the Atlantic World* (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2020). She is co-director of the Diaspora Solidarities Lab, which is a multi-institutional Black feminist partnership that supports solidarity work in Black and Ethnic Studies that is both analog and digital. She also founded the LifeXCode project, which is a digital humanities initiative that explores the intersections of Black life and code. 

Core questions today:

- How does the history of slavery help us see some of the issues with trying to digitize or create digital archives? 
- How do we handle the issue of missingness in data?
- What older histories of counting and classification does digital data inherit?
::::

## Why title the article "Markup Bodies"? 
::: {.r-fit-text .fragment}

> "In the United States, historians of slavery have made particular use of digital tools to document the forced migration of black women, children, and men throughout the Atlantic littoral over the last five centuries. In 1974, Eugene Genovese coined the phrase “the world the slaves made” to describe the political economy, society, and culture of the antebellum South. Over four decades later, scholars struggle to translate “the world the slaves made” into code and express it in technical language. From blogs and journals built on fourth-generation hypertext markup language (HTML) guided by cascading style sheets (CSS) to databases using extensible markup language (XML) and standard query language (SQL), [**scholars using digital tools mark up the bodies and requantify the
lives of people of African descent**.]{bg="#d7ecff"}" (emphasis added) p. 59
:::
::: {.notes}
Given this quote what do you think the main focus of this article is? What is the author trying to argue about the history of slavery and the digital humanities? How does this relate to the history of datafication and digitization? What is the relationship between bodies, data, and code?
:::

## Is data ever objective or neutral? 

[![](../assets/images/data_ngram.png)](https://books.google.com/ngrams/graph?content=data%2Cdigital%2Cinformation%2Cknowledge&year_start=1800&year_end=2022&corpus=en&smoothing=3){target="_blank"}

How does Prof. Johnson define data?

> "Data, defined here as an objective and independent unit of knowledge, has been central to the architecture of both slavery studies and digital humanistic study."
> 
> "However, in this article I question the stability of what has been or can be categorized as data, the uses the idea of data has been put to, and the stakes underlying data’s implicit claim to stability or objectivity. This article uses the term data transhistorically to gesture to the rise of the independent and objective statistical fact as an explanatory ideal party to the devastating thingification of black women, children, and men." p. 58

Why do we tend to think of it that way? Where does data even come from as a concept?

- What is the difference between datafication and digitization?
- What are some of the historic ways that culture or people have been turned into data that you know about?
- When do you think datafication first began? What are some of the earliest examples you can think of? 
Culture becomes data long before it becomes digital.

- People get named, counted, classified, measured, and compared
- Institutions decide what counts as evidence
- Records move into archives, ledgers, tables, maps, databases, and interfaces
- Each transformation changes what culture can mean

What could looking at a google ngram tell us about the history of the word data?
:::

## A Short History of the Word “Data”

[![Rosenberg, Daniel. 2013. “‘Data before the Fact.’” In *Raw Data Is an Oxymoron*. Edited by Lisa Gitelman. MIT Press.](../assets/images/data_rosenberg.png)](https://direct.mit.edu/books/edited-volume/3992/chapter-abstract/166412/Data-before-the-Fact?redirectedFrom=fulltext){target="_blank"}


::: {.notes}

Daniel Rosenberg argues that “data” did not begin with computers.

- English uses of “data” appear in the seventeenth century
- The term comes from Latin *datum*: something “given”
- Data originally meant something accepted as a starting point in argument
- Data is related to facts and evidence, but not identical to either

This matters because “data” has never simply meant neutral truth. Rosenberg argues that data has long had a rhetorical function: it names what is given so an argument can proceed. That makes Johnson’s critique especially powerful. When Neptune’s death becomes data, it is not only recorded. It is made into a premise for argument.

Data originally meant “a given”
- From Latin datum, from dare, “to give.”
- A datum is something granted or accepted as a starting point.

A given is not the same as a fact
- A fact makes a claim about what happened or exists.
- Evidence helps prove or support a claim.
- Data is what gets treated as given so an argument can proceed.
- This means data can be false, partial, violent, or misleading and still function as data.

The word takes off later because it was adaptable
- Rosenberg argues the term becomes more familiar in the eighteenth century, but the major takeoff is nineteenth/twentieth century.
- Computing and information theory gave “data” new importance.
- But the older rhetorical structure remained: data still names what a system, argument, or analysis treats as input.
:::

## Tabulation Technologies & Thingification

[![](../assets/images/mason_ledger_loc.jpg)](https://blogs.loc.gov/manuscripts/2023/12/a-new-look-at-an-old-ledger-reveals-stories-about-african-american-history/){target="_blank"}

::: {.notes}
At the back of the ledger, where the pages are unnumbered, is a list headed: “Inventory of slaves stock &c. in the estate of the late Col. Richard Barnes in Washington County on the 15th May 1804.” It includes names, ages, and deaths, and mentions “papers,” for some – probably a reference to the legal papers that “manumitted,” or freed them. Unheaded lists on several subsequent pages also seem to refer to the people freed by Barnes, as well as others still enslaved. These note names, ages, family relationships in some cases, and indicate some who were sold. Also at the back of the book are lists recording the names and ages of enslaved people Mason hired out to work for others in 1806 and 1807. There are, in addition, scrawled notes on the endpapers of the ledger with additional information about the operation of the farm and the people who worked on it.
:::

## 19th Century Tabulating Machines

[![Hollerith Tabulating Machine](https://ietarchivesblog.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/08/naest-233-03-page-08-image-of-hollerith-tabulator.jpg)](https://ietarchivesblog.org/2015/08/12/the-history-of-computing-tabulating-machines/){target="_blank"}

::: {.notes}
Hollerith started his own business in 1896, founding the Tabulating Machine Company. In 1911, 4 corporations, including Hollerith’s firm merged to form the Computing Tabulating Recording Company (CTR) and in 1924 CTR was renamed International Business Machines (IBM). A Hollerith tabulator illustrated in a 1929 booklet is shown below.

Invented by Hermann Hollerith, the machine was developed to help process data for the 1890 US Census. It led to a class of machines, known as unit record equipment, and the data processing industry. The term ‘Super Computing’ was used by the New York World newspaper in 1931 to refer to large custom-built tabulator that IBM made for Columbia University.

Herman Hollerith’s tabulating machine was a punch card system that allowed the U.S. Census Bureau to process data more quickly and efficiently. It was used for the 1890 census and was a precursor to modern computing. The machine used punched cards to represent data, which could then be read and processed by the machine. This technology was a significant advancement in data processing and laid the groundwork for future developments in computing and data analysis. It also reflects the broader trend of datafication in the 19th century, where information about people and society was increasingly being collected, categorized, and analyzed for various purposes, including governance, research, and commerce.

[![Barrett, Alec and TWO-N. “The Evolution of the American Census.” *The Pudding*.](https://pudding.cool/2020/03/census-history/assets/social/social-twitter.jpg)](https://pudding.cool/2020/03/census-history/){target="_blank"}
:::

## What was the problem with Cliometrics?
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%" }
[![](https://m.media-amazon.com/images/I/51ppTVCitKL._AC_UF1000,1000_QL80_.jpg)](https://dhdebates.gc.cuny.edu/read/computational-humanities-5c64bbab-d7ca-41be-8f87-f26117a9a20f/section/158d174a-0e45-4e37-82a4-3dbeadd223b2){target="_blank"}
:::

::: {.column width="60%" .r-fit-text}
> **Statistics on their own, enticing in their seeming neutrality, failed to address or unpack black life hidden behind the archetypes, caricatures, and nameless numbered registers of human property.** p. 61
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The impulse to revisit the plantation South from the perspective of black laborers and their experi- ences contributed to changing conceptions of data as historians struggled with which sources would be of value, what meaning could be gleaned from narratives and numbers, and what archival material appeared to be stable, objective, and quanti "able → In the 1970s, a subset of cliometricians, a cohort of researchers using statistics to write economic studies of history, grew especially interested in the slavery debates. Cliometricians paid special interest to quantifying the lives of the enslaved but were motivated by very qualitative consider- ations — the tense and emotional tenor of the topic. In later years, Robert Fogel,  coauthor  with  Stanley  Engerman  of  Time  on  the  Cross:  The  Eco- nomics of Negro Slavery, described the cliometric struggle with slavery as emerging from a “desire to develop a precise, emotionally detached, ideo- logically neutral analysis. When Fogel and Engerman applied statistical methods to their data, they concluded that the material lives of enslaved black women, children, and men were better, on average, than those of twentieth-century African Americans. In fact, in their estimation, slavery was an efficient and modern economic institution, quite compatible with “shifting labor requirements of capitalist society.→ An indignant Herbert Gutman published expressive critiques of their strategy. In Slavery and the Numbers Game:
A Critique of “Time on the Cross,” Gutman identified the methodological problem as a “model [that] mixes two processes together: how slaves learned and what slaves learned.”15 Statistics on their own, enticing in their seeming neutrality, failed to address or unpack black life hidden behind the archetypes, caricatures, and nameless numbered registers of human property slave owners had left behind. And cliometricians failed to remove emotion from the discussion. Data without an accompanying humanistic analysis — an exploration of the world of the enslaved from their own perspective — served to further obscure the social and political realities of black diasporic life under slavery.
:::

::: {.notes}
Origins and Early Digital Era (1983–1999)1983: Ancestry Publishing is founded, producing family history magazines and genealogy guides.1990: Founders Paul Brent Allen and Dan Taggart establish Infobases, selling Latter-day Saints publications and early genealogical databases on floppy disks and CDs.1996: Ancestry.com officially launches online as a digital database for family history.1997: Western Standard Publishing (Infobases' parent company) acquires Ancestry, Inc.1998: The company launches MyFamily.com, expanding into broader online family networking. Expansion and Digital Milestones (2000–2012)2000–2003: Ancestry begins publishing digitized historical census data, completing the 1930 U.S. Federal Census index in 2003. 2001: The platform launches its first international site, Ancestry.co.uk, expanding further into Australia, Canada, Germany, and other European countries through the mid-2000s. 2006: Features like "shaky leaf" hints and Ancestry Member Trees are introduced to simplify collaborative tree-building. 2009: The company rebrands fully to Ancestry.com and goes public with an initial public offering (IPO) on NASDAQ. 
2012: Ancestry introduces AncestryDNA, blending historical records with consumer genetic testing. Later that year, private equity firm Permira acquires a majority stake, valuing the company at $1.6 billion. Recent Ownership and Growth (2013–Present)2013: Ancestry acquires the popular grave and memorial database Find a Grave. 
2016–2020: Private equity firms Silver Lake and GIC increase their investments, leading up to a major acquisition by Blackstone in 2020 at an enterprise value of $4.7 billion.

What is the difference between public history and a for-profit company? Does anyone remember digital history?
:::

## W.E.B. Du Bois and the 1900 Paris Exposition

[![](https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/pnp/ppmsca/33800/33893r.jpg)](https://www.loc.gov/pictures/collection/anedub/dubois.html){target="_blank"}

For more on the visualizations, see Forrest, Jason. 2018. “W. E. B. Du Bois’ Staggering Data Visualizations Are as Powerful Today as They Were in 1900 (Part 1), Nightingale.” Nightingale, June 18. [https://nightingaledvs.com/w-e-b-du-bois-staggering-data-visualizations-are-as-powerful-today-as-they-were-in-1900-part-1/](https://nightingaledvs.com/w-e-b-du-bois-staggering-data-visualizations-are-as-powerful-today-as-they-were-in-1900-part-1/){target="_blank"}.

::: {.notes}
I want to pause here because Du Bois gives us a different way to think about data, history, and visual argument.

For the 1900 Paris Exposition, Du Bois and his collaborators created a series of data visualizations about Black life in the United States, especially in Georgia. These were made only a few decades after emancipation, in a context where racist science and racist public culture were actively trying to define Black people as inferior.

So these visualizations are not neutral charts. They are arguments. They use data, design, color, and comparison to make Black social life visible on different terms. They show education, property ownership, occupations, literacy, population change, and institutional life.

This is useful for us because it complicates the question of whether data is always dehumanizing. Du Bois shows that data can be used against racist narratives, but only when the categories, context, and visual forms are doing careful interpretive work.
:::

## Afrofuturism Listserv

[![](../assets/images/afrofuturism_listserv.png)](https://web.archive.org/web/20010719155250/http://www.afrofuturism.net/text/about.html){target="_blank"}

::: {.notes}
I also want to bring in the Afrofuturism listserv because it helps us move from data visualization to digital community and digital history.

In the 1990s, before social media as we know it, listservs were one of the main ways people built intellectual communities online. The Afrofuturism listserv brought together writers, artists, scholars, and technologists interested in Black futures, science fiction, technology, music, and speculative culture.

Alondra Nelson was one of the important figures in this space. Her work helped frame Afrofuturism not just as an aesthetic, but as a way to think critically about race, technology, history, and the future. In other words, Black digital practice was not only about recovering the past. It was also about imagining different technological futures.

This gives us another answer to Johnson’s question. If damaging archives can reproduce harm in digital systems, then Black digital practice can also create alternative infrastructures: spaces for community, memory, critique, creativity, and future-making.
:::

## Black Digital Practice & Future

> **The study of black life and culture must also accompany an ethical and moral concern with sustaining black life and shaping black futures**

A corrective that:

- Centers descendants and their needs
- Embraces the uncomfortable and unquantifiable
- Refuses disposability
- Infuses data work with humanity

## Black Digital Practice and Missingness

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
[![Hartman, Saidiya. 2008. “Venus in Two Acts.” Small Axe: A Caribbean Journal of Criticism 12 (2): 1–14](https://encrypted-tbn0.gstatic.com/images?q=tbn:ANd9GcS7e48OQL7BdJv61tKX13oTKt3bKWZpuKQQQxZDqmi_CLhs95-1vsGyMCA&s=10)](https://doi.org/10.1215/-12-2-1){target="_blank"}

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
[![Saidiya Hartman](https://www.amacad.org/sites/default/files/person/headshots/Hartman%20from%20Columbia%20faculty%20page.png)](https://english.columbia.edu/content/saidiya-v-hartman){target="_blank"}
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Sadiya Hartman’s essay “Venus in Two Acts” is a powerful example of how to handle missingness in historical research. She explores the lives of enslaved women, particularly focusing on the gaps and silences in the historical record. Hartman argues that these absences are not just gaps in knowledge but are themselves meaningful, revealing the violence and erasure inherent in the history of slavery. By acknowledging and engaging with these silences, Hartman demonstrates a method of historical inquiry that respects the humanity of those who have been marginalized and whose stories have often been left untold. This approach aligns with the principles of Black digital practice, emphasizing the importance of centering marginalized voices and experiences in research and data representation.
:::

# Semester Long Project Discussion

- Initial Collective and Individual topic selection due today! Extension available until next Tuesday.

Let's discuss project requirements!

## Pivoting Is Allowed

- The topic selection is pass/fail intentionally to let you explore topics without worrying about grades.
- Goal is to try and make a broad plan for your semester project, not to have a final plan.
- Requires you thinking about three components:
  - Group topic & website
  - Individually creating a dataset
  - Individually auditing a dataset

## For Group Work

- You should try and find a collective topic that is broad but not so broad to just be cultural data.
- Think about different ways to draw connections between your group members’ indi`vidual datasets.
- We will discuss final website and GitHub repository requirements in the upcoming weeks.


*If you are struggling to find a collective topic, please reach out to the instructors for guidance.*



## For individual work

Your custom created dataset needs to involve the following components:

- Should relate to your group topic
- Should try to capture cultural complexity and interpretative subjectivity
- Should involve some form of computation beyond a spreadsheet

## What is cultural complexity?

For your semester project, **cultural complexity** means your dataset should capture more than the easiest categories.

It might include:

- Ambiguity, uncertainty, or conflicting interpretations
- Context around genre, platform, audience, circulation, or reception
- Relationships among people, objects, places, institutions, and events
- Evidence of absences, silences, or limits
- Notes on categories that do not quite fit

::: {.notes}
I want to push them beyond title, date, author, and URL. Those fields can matter, but they often do not capture why the cultural object is interesting. The goal is for students to ask what they wish the dataset could preserve about the cultural phenomenon.
:::

## What is subjectivity?

A strong cultural dataset does not pretend interpretation disappears.

Instead, it documents:

- Who made the data
- What choices shaped the fields
- What evidence supports each category
- What remains uncertain
- What another person might classify differently

::: {.notes}
This is where Johnson matters for the assignment. Students are going to make interpretive choices no matter what. The question is whether they make those choices visible and responsible.
:::

## Computation Beyond a Spreadsheet

Computation does not have to mean advanced programming.

It can mean using code or digital tools to:

- Extract text from images or PDFs
- Create an HTML page for curating objects
- Check consistency across records
- Compare categories or sources
- Identify missing values
- Create a simple visualization
- Transform messy data into reusable data

::: {.notes}
This is a place to lower the intimidation level while also raising the bar beyond manually filling a spreadsheet. A spreadsheet can be part of the workflow, but they should use computation to structure, check, compare, publish, or question their data.
:::

## Making Transformation Visible

Your project should show at least two transformations:

1. Cultural material becomes a working representation
2. The representation becomes structured data

Examples:

- A magazine page becomes a scan, then OCR text, then coded records
- A TikTok becomes a screenshot and transcript, then thematic annotations
- A museum object becomes catalog metadata, then a revised data record
- A sports article becomes saved text, then fields about source, rhetoric, and event

::: {.notes}
This language comes directly from the semester project. I want them to see that the assignment is not asking for magic. It is asking them to make visible how culture changes form as it becomes data.
:::

## Before You Build a Dataset

Ask:

- What cultural complexity am I trying to preserve?
- What older categories or systems does my source inherit?
- What can computation help me see or check?
- What can computation not understand on its own?
- What documentation would help someone reuse this responsibly?

::: {.notes}
This is the practical takeaway. If students can answer these questions, they are already moving toward a stronger proposal and a stronger mid-semester custom dataset.
:::
